extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, judges, government and military officials, legal researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing creation, appointment, acceptance, vesting, vacation, dismissal, and eligibility for public and military offices in the United States (including volunteers and cadet appointments). Primarily a legal reference summarizing statutes, Attorney General opinions, and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a public office
rubrics_metrics.description: A public office is a place created by statute or by virtue of a power conferred by statute for administration of public affairs, the holder of which is appointed or elected and not employed merely by contract; duties are continuing and permanent and defined by government rules, not contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities and cases (U.S. v. Hartwell; U.S. v. Germaine; Sheboygan Co. v. Parker). Emphasizes tenure, duration, emolument, and continuing duties as essential features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of offices must be by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices in the military establishment are created by law; the Executive has no authority to establish or maintain offices not expressly provided by Congress or authorized by law (expressly or by necessary implication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites opinions and decisions (e.g., C.15844 Jan. 21, 1904). Illustrative historical example: Maj. Gen. Fremont had no power to create offices during Civil War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prescribe incidents of an office
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to create an office includes the power to prescribe necessary incidents of such office (tenure, salary, emoluments, and within limits, conditions of eligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive can set these incident terms when law creates an office (C.23122, Apr. 22, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting of office occurs on acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule in original appointments, the office vests on the date of its acceptance by the appointee, even if the oath of office is taken afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and examples (C.23668; 4567; 6644). Acceptance may be express or implied; vesting date fixes rights such as pay and seniority unless statute provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance may be express or implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of office may be 'express' (formal written acceptance) or 'implied' (by entering upon performance of duties or equivalent acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mailing an acceptance (C.16732) or entering on duties; cadet academy signature of articles may substitute for formal acceptance (special rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of acceptance fixes effective date and pay (with limited exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of acceptance generally fixes the date of vesting (and related rights such as pay), though remedial legislation may grant pay for service prior to acceptance in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example where remedial legislation gave pay for service prior to acceptance; see Page 824 notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting rules differ for graduates/cadets
rubrics_metrics.description: A Military Academy graduate who has signed required articles may have the office vest without a separate formal acceptance; cadet-specific rules can displace normal acceptance formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case C.27241: cadet who signed articles vested without formal acceptance; special statutes (sec.1321,1325 R.S.) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting on promotion conditioned on acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: In promotions, an office vests on the date of the appointment or commission on condition that the appointment/commission is thereafter accepted; without acceptance (even if Senate confirmed) the office does not vest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where death before acceptance meant no vesting (C.28369, C.16359).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointment authority and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may fill vacancies during the Senate recess by granting commissions (recess appointments) which expire at the end of the Senate's next session; the President's recess appointment power is independent and not limited to vacancies that arose during the recess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites constitutional provision (Art. II, sec.2, par.3) and multiple Attorney General opinions; Senate rejection of a nomination does not automatically oust a recess appointee for the remainder of the allowed term (C.9096).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification methods and constructive notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Notification of acceptance or other appointment actions can be constructive; constructive notification (e.g., appointment of successor) may suffice to effect vesting or acceptance status for purposes of resignation/acceptance rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance may become operative through constructive acts; see discussion under resignation acceptance (notification of acceptance: constructive notification; by appointment of successor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation acceptance can be refused and may be delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: A resignation may be refused; the power to accept resignation may be delegated; an acceptance when notified has specific legal effects and may be irrevocable after notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints: (a) may be refused; (b) power may be delegated; (c) notification of acceptance (constructive or appointment of successor); (d) not revocable after notification—even if acceptance is in futuro; remarks in acceptance; acceptance of resignation has procedural nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation may be revoked before acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: A resignation may be revoked before it is accepted by the appropriate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'By Resignation — May be revoked before acceptance' with citation to earlier pages/sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal by court-martial: date and finality
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal by sentence of a court-martial: the date of confirmation of the sentence fixes the date of dismissal; prior dates cannot be fixed; a legal dismissal is irrevocable, and if illegal the office is not vacated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include failure of notification due to capture by enemy; de facto officers may be mustered in to replace illegally dismissed officers (Cites pages and cases). Dismissal does not necessarily render the person ineligible for future appointment or enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal by order of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: When removed by order of the President, the removal takes effect as of the date of notification; such removals are generally irrevocable and have defined effects on status and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints: whether antecedent advisory board members were sworn; notification date and fixing of date; removal by inferior officers (Secretary of War); character and consequences discussed (e.g., does not render ineligible for appointment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacation of office for failure to pass examination after promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer may vacate an office by failing to pass a required examination after promotion when the promotion is subject to examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a specific ground for vacation of office; related to qualifying examinations and suspensions from promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple grounds for vacation of office (volunteers and regulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices may be vacated by accepting another office, by abandoning office, by summary dismissal, by abolishing the office, or by sentence of a general court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically noted for volunteer officers as well as regulars; also notes special rules about holding two offices concurrently in some combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding two offices concurrently in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Two offices may be held without vacating either in certain situations: (1) a public civil officer may accept a volunteer commission; (2) a volunteer officer may hold a Regular Army office—rules depend on which office vested first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and distinctions where regular office vesting first vs volunteer office vesting first are given (Page 826).

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto officers' acts are valid as to third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A de facto officer's acts are lawful as far as the rights of third persons are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to protect third-party rights when an officer's appointment is later questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and modes of advancement (promotion vs appointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advancement in the military establishment occurs either by promotion (within the line or staff) or by appointment (selection, nomination, confirmation); the Military Academy graduating class is recognized as primary source for lowest commissioned grades, with enlisted competition filling remaining vacancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutes and opinions (C.19425; acts and cases). Explains order of eligibility among academy graduates, enlisted men, civilians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility timing rules: age, citizenship, service, and physical qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rules include: age limits apply at date of commission (not earlier); enlisted competitors must have served required time (e.g., two years counted with furloughs included); citizenship/naturalization requirements may apply (naturalization may be required before appointment); physical disqualification, marriage or failure to reenlist can forfeit a Certificate of Eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutory and case citations: act of July 30, 1892 (service and age rules), C.20639 on limiting age at date of issue of commission, and citations re naturalization and reenlistment (P.57 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of competitive examinations and counting of failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute may limit number of examinations accorded to the same competitor (e.g., no more than two); physical examination failures are preliminary and do not count as one of the statutory 'examinations' limiting attempts—two failures of the competitive mental examination render a candidate ineligible for further examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.9521 Jan. 1901 and statutory references; distinction between physical and mental exams is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reappointment/restoration rules and presidential vs congressional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration to command or reinstatement (e.g., an officer pardoned and 'restored to his former rank and position') may amount to a new appointment; Congress may authorize the President to reappoint or restore an officer without Senate concurrence in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Presidential pardon language that did not produce vesting when the regiment had been mustered out; acts of Congress that empowered the President to reinstate without Senate (C.18785 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to administer oaths is statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to administer oaths must be conferred by law; neither a major general commanding nor the Secretary of War can authorize administering oaths except as provided by law; certain officers (judge advocates, trial officers of summary courts) are authorized by statute to administer oaths for military administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutory provisions (act of July 27, 1892; section 183 R.S., act of May 28, 1896) and cases noting who may/cannot administer oaths (postmaster not competent for army officer oath, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers generally have no power virtute officii to administer oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Army has no authority by virtue of his office alone to administer an oath; specific statutory grants are required to do so in certain contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions enumerated (second, eighty-fourth, eighty-fifth articles of war; section 183 R.S.; judge advocates authorized under statutory acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: President cannot exceed statutory numbers or create offices by appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The President cannot appoint a greater number of officers to a grade than fixed by law, nor can the President create offices by appointment; appointments cannot be made by legislative enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Montgomery v. U.S. and other authorities. Emphasizes constitutional limits on the appointing power and Congressional prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion by seniority and the effect of suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion by seniority is required by statute (e.g., act of Oct. 1, 1890); suspension from promotion (e.g., for failure to pass examination) is a penalty that runs for one year and until a qualifying vacancy occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.15028 and related citations: suspension operative when right to promotion would have accrued; suspension effects and duration described.

rubrics_metrics.name: No absolute vested right to promotion; Congress may alter seniority
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no inherent vested right in promotion beyond rights conferred by existing law; Congress may change commission dates or otherwise legislate to affect seniority and promotion rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where Congress authorized a new commission date to change promotion precedence; such legislation is within Congressional power and construed as a requirement on the President in execution (P.58-309).
